## Learning objectives

Before the timed session, you should be able to open the workshop project,
identify its source data, and load a verified copy in R. You will use the same
project and dataset throughout the workshop.

Allow time for downloads and setup before the session. Some familiarity with R
is helpful; you do not need previous experience with meta-analysis.

## Our teaching dataset

We use `HealthWellbeing` from section **4.2.4, Correlations**, of
[*Doing Meta-Analysis with R: A Hands-On Guide*](https://doing-meta.guide/pooling-es#correlations).
It contains study-level summaries of the association between health and
well-being. It is also distributed with the `dmetar` package.

The original review is Ngamaba, Panagioti, and Armitage (2017). Consult the
[dataset documentation](https://dmetar.protectlab.org/reference/healthwellbeing)
for the variable definitions and original reference.

We will download the authors' data file directly, so these opening activities
do not require installation of `dmetar`. Keep the raw file unchanged and record
its source separately from any transformations you make later.

## Choose your computing environment

Use one of these routes:

- **Local R:** install R and an editor such as RStudio. The reference environment
  uses **R 4.4.1**. Record any difference if you use another version.
- **Docker:** use the workshop RStudio image confirmed by the instructor.
  Follow the [Docker instructions](03_environments.qmd#environments-docker)
  before the session; downloading an image can take time.

Both routes need Git for the local version-control activity. A GitHub account
lets you practise sharing from your own fork. Install Quarto before the session
if you will render reports locally later; HTML reporting does not require LaTeX.

Browser-based Binder access is still being prepared. Use a verified local or
Docker environment for this workshop.

## Current development status

The committed lockfile records renv 1.0.7. For lessons 04–07, use
the instructor's prepared environment with `box`, `codebook`,
`dataspice`, `pins`, `targets`, `meta`, `visNetwork`, `knitr`, and
`rmarkdown`. Ask about `synthpop` and `vetiver` if you plan to run
the optional exercises. On Linux, building the `dataspice`
dependency `jqr` from source needs the jq development library.

Run the lesson chunks in the R Console. Use Quarto with `knitr` and
`rmarkdown` when you are ready to render the standalone report.

## Get your own project copy

1. Open the [workshop repository](https://github.com/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r)
   and use **Fork** to create a copy in your GitHub account.
2. In your fork, select **Code**, copy its HTTPS clone URL, and clone it with Git.
   Replace `YOUR-USERNAME` below with your GitHub username.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r.git
cd open-and-reproducible-science-in-r
```

Open `open-and-reproducible-science-in-r.Rproj` in RStudio. For Docker, open the
project in the mounted checkout described in the environment chapter. Keep
terminal commands and R Console commands rooted in this project directory.

The project's `.Rprofile` activates renv; first startup may download renv.
Complete that startup and any restoration before the session. In the R Console:

```{r health-preparation-environment, include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, cache = TRUE, output = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
R.version.string
renv::restore()
renv::status()
```

Restoration installs packages recorded in the lockfile. It does not supply
unrecorded workshop packages or install the R version named by the lockfile.

## Download and verify the raw data {#preparation-data}

Run the following in the **R Console** from the project root. The R chunks
are also configured to run during rendering; setup chunks are uncached and
other R chunks use the cache.

The download comes from the resource linked in the book. The checksum identifies
the exact file used to prepare these lessons. If you already have a different
copy, keep it and ask the instructor to resolve the difference.

```{r health-preparation-download, include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, cache = TRUE, output = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
raw_file <- file.path("data", "raw", "healthwellbeing.rda")
source_url <- paste0(
  "https://www.protectlab.org/meta-analysis-in-r/data/",
  "healthwellbeing.rda"
)

dir.create(dirname(raw_file), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
if (!file.exists(raw_file)) {
  download.file(source_url, destfile = raw_file, mode = "wb")
}

expected_md5 <- "0d74964b0b7168379a2b015cb648b326"
actual_md5 <- unname(tools::md5sum(raw_file))
stopifnot(identical(actual_md5, expected_md5))
actual_md5
```

Load into a separate environment so the file does not silently replace objects
in your working session. Use an explicit name for the dataset you will inspect.

```{r health-preparation-load, include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, cache = TRUE, output = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
data_env <- new.env(parent = baseenv())
loaded_names <- load(raw_file, envir = data_env)
stopifnot(identical(loaded_names, "HealthWellbeing"))
health <- data_env[["HealthWellbeing"]]

expected_columns <- c("author", "cor", "n", "population", "country")
stopifnot(
  is.data.frame(health),
  nrow(health) == 29L,
  identical(names(health), expected_columns),
  !anyNA(health),
  all(is.finite(health$cor)),
  all(abs(health$cor) < 1),
  all(is.finite(health$n)),
  all(health$n > 3),
  all(health$n == floor(health$n))
)

head(health, 3)
dim(health)
```

Expected checkpoint: **29 rows and 5 columns**, with no assertion failures.
These checks describe this teaching snapshot, not a general rule that all
meta-analysis datasets must be complete or have this size.

If downloading is unavailable, ask for the instructor's prepared copy, put it
at the same project-relative path, and run the checksum and loading checks.

## Record the source

For your project notes, retain the book section, dataset documentation, download
URL, retrieval date, checksum, and original study citation. A package licence or
the workshop repository's MIT licence should not be assumed to relicense every
upstream dataset; check the relevant reuse terms before redistributing data.

We will create and commit a short provenance note in the
[Git and GitHub activity](02_git_github.qmd).

## Preparation checkpoint {#preparation-checkpoint}

You are ready when:

- The project opens in your chosen environment and Git is available.
- You know your R version and have completed the initial renv startup.
- The raw file is saved and its checksum matches the teaching snapshot.
- `health` contains the verified data, and you can identify its upstream source.

Continue to [open and reproducible science](01_open_science.qmd).

## Further reading

Harrer, M., Cuijpers, P., Furukawa, T. A., & Ebert, D. D. (2021).
*Doing Meta-Analysis with R: A Hands-On Guide*. Chapman & Hall/CRC.
[Section 4.2.4](https://doing-meta.guide/pooling-es#correlations).

Ngamaba, K. H., Panagioti, M., & Armitage, C. J. (2017).
How strongly related are health status and subjective well-being? Systematic
review and meta-analysis. *The European Journal of Public Health*, 27(5), 879–885.
